    %% Layer 1: User/Client
    U["User/Client"]:::user

    CI["CLI Interface"]:::core
    WA["Web API/Monitoring"]:::interface
    VU["Version Utility"]:::core

    CA["Core Application Module"]:::core
    CFG["Configuration Module"]:::config
    PS["Plugin System"]:::plugin

    %% Layer 4: Tunneling Logic
    TE["Tunneling Engine"]:::engine
    FP["Forward Proxy"]:::engine
    PF["Port Forwarding"]:::engine
    RP["Reverse Proxy"]:::engine

    GH["GitHub Workflows"]:::integration
    DF["Dockerfile"]:::integration
    GR[".goreleaser.yaml"]:::integration
    MK["Makefile"]:::integration

    %% Connections from User/Client to Input Interfaces
    U -->|"starts"| CI
    U -->|"requests"| WA
    U -->|"version inquiry"| VU

    %% Input Interfaces feed into the Core Application Module
    CI -->|"executes"| CA
    VU --> CA
    WA --> CA

    %% Configuration Module loads and supplies data to Core Application Module
    CFG -->|"loads config"| CA

    %% Core Application Module triggers Tunneling Engine and Plugin System
    CA -->|"initializes"| TE

    %% Tunneling Engine branches into different modes
    TE -->|"handles"| FP
    TE -->|"handles"| PF
    TE -->|"handles"| RP

    %% Tunneling Engine feeds back monitoring data to Web API/Monitoring
    TE -->|"metrics"| WA

    %% External Integrations deploy and build the Core Application Module
    GH -->|"CI/CD triggers"| CA
    DF --> CA
    GR --> CA
    MK --> CA

<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README provided, here’s how to produce a detailed system design diagram that reflects GO Simple Tunnel’s architecture:

1. Project Type and Purpose
   • This is a Go-based command-line application that implements a secure tunnel (proxy/tunneling) with multi-protocol support. It can be used in different modes (forward proxy, port forwarding, reverse proxy) and is intended to provide secure, flexible network tunneling capabilities.
   • The README shows that the system supports a range of functionalities—from multi-port listening to plugins, routing control, dynamic configuration, and integrated APIs/GUI. This tells us that both the core tunneling engine and its extensibility are fundamental to the design.

2. Analyzing the File Structure
   • The project has a single executable command in the “cmd/gost” directory, where main.go acts as the entry point and auxiliary files (program.go, register.go, version.go) subdivide functionality for program initialization, registration of modules or protocols, and version management.
   • Build and deployment support is evident from files such as Dockerfile, .goreleaser.yaml, Makefile, as well as GitHub workflows in the “.github/workflows” directory. This indicates a well-structured CI/CD and release process.
   • The existence of “gost.yml” suggests that the application supports external configuration, impacting how the tunnel chains are built or managed.

3. Architectural Components to Include
   • Core Application Module: Represented by the cmd/gost component where the main application logic lives.
   • Configuration Module: Read configuration data (from gost.yml and dynamic configurations via the API) to control tunnel behavior.
   • Tunneling Engine: Core logic that enables multi-level forwarding chain, protocol handling (TCP/UDP, DNS, etc.), and various tunneling modes (forward, reverse, port forwarding).
   • Plugin System: Extendable architecture to allow additional functionalities such as routing control, limits, custom protocols, and integration with GUIs/WebUI.
   • Web API/Monitoring: Components to handle Prometheus metrics, dynamic configuration, and the Web API to interact via HTTP.
   • External Integrations: Docker support for container deployments and CI/CD pipelines to support automated building and releases.
   • CLI and Utility Components: Parts of the system dealing with command-line parsing and version/reporting, as seen in register.go and version.go.

4. Relationships and Data Flow
   • Draw a primary flow from user/client requests (either via CLI commands, web requests, or through GUI/WebUI integrations) entering the system.
   • Show that configuration data is loaded early in the application lifecycle, which then configures the tunneling engine.
   • Illustrate how the core tunneling engine directs data through the appropriate protocol chains based on the configuration: e.g., separate branches or nodes for forward proxy, port forwarding, and reverse proxy modes.
   • Indicate interactions with external modules such as plugins, external monitoring (Prometheus), and the web API interface. 
   • Mark communications and dependencies from external clients to the secure tunnel endpoints.

5. Design Guidelines Tailored to This Project
   • Since this is a full-fledged tunneling solution with multiple operational modes, your diagram should separately highlight the three major usage scenarios:
     - Forward Proxy: Show how the tunnel receives requests and chains multiple protocol handlers.
     - Port Forwarding: Illustrate the mapping process from an incoming port to the respective destination.
     - Reverse Proxy: Depict the mechanism for exposing internal services to external endpoints.
   • Emphasize modularity — clearly demonstrate how the plugin system, configuration module, and tunneling engine operate independently but interact through well-defined interfaces.
   • Identify integration points with deployment and monitoring pieces (like Docker containers, CI workflows, and metrics collection).

6. Diagram Elements to Use
   • Clearly label each component (e.g., “Main Application,” “Configuration Parser,” “Tunneling Engine,” “Plugin Manager,” “Web API/Monitoring”).
   • Use directional arrows to denote the flow of control/data (for example, from configuration loading to tunneling engine initialization, and between protocol chain modules).
   • Apply color coding or shape distinctions to group similar layer types – for example, one color for core engine pieces (tunneling engine, configuration), another for external interfaces (CLI, Web API, Docker & CI/CD), and a third for auxiliary plugins/extensions.
   • Optionally, include icons or annotations that indicate deployment (Docker, GitHub Actions) vs. runtime components.

7. Final Notes for the Principal Software Engineer
   • Stay detailed—capture not only the high-level modules but also the interactions such as how internal protocol selections are determined by configuration and the dynamic linking to plugins.
   • Avoid over-complicating the diagram; instead, strive for clarity by separating the architectural elements into distinct zones: startup/configuration, tunneling logic, plugin/extensions, and external interfaces.
   • Ensure that all components mentioned are clearly represented along with their interactions, and include annotations where necessary (for instance, note “handles TCP/UDP redirection” near the tunneling engine).

By following these guidelines, your system design diagram will provide a thorough and accurate architectural overview of the GO Simple Tunnel project, capturing both its internal structure and its integration with external systems. 
</explanation>
